game_title: Commanders of the Cosmos: Mars Exploration Odyssey

questions.story: Welcome to the Mars Flight Control Center, Commander! Your robotic probe has separated from its interplanetary transfer stage and is coasting toward Mars at 21,000 km/h.
questions.question: Which orbital insertion strategy will you command?

source.title: NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Aerobraking Campaign

answers.text: Perform a gradual aerobraking campaign using upper atmospheric drag.
answers.consequence_summary: Saves 600 kg of heavy retro-rocket propellant, though high temperatures test thermal tile limits.
answers.learning_point: Aerobraking converts kinetic energy into heat by grazing the atmosphere over hundreds of orbits, saving massive amounts of rocket fuel.

answers.text: Execute a high-thrust bipropellant rocket burn for immediate orbit capture.
answers.consequence_summary: Puts your spacecraft into science orbit instantly, but burns through huge amounts of fuel mass and budget.
answers.learning_point: Direct propulsive burns require carrying heavy chemical fuel, which increases the launch rocket class needed.

questions.story: During aerobraking, orbital friction heats your leading solar array edges. You must maintain electrical generation while protecting delicate solar cells.
questions.question: How will you adjust the solar wing orientation during atmospheric passes?

source.title: NASA Mars Odyssey Mission Aerobraking Architecture

answers.text: Feather the arrays edge-on to the wind to minimize friction drag and heat.
answers.consequence_summary: Reduces aerodynamic stress and protects panels, settling safely into low science orbit.
answers.learning_point: Feathering solar panels reduces surface area exposed to supersonic gas drag, preventing structural bending.

answers.text: Keep arrays flat to brake faster, counting on internal radiative cooling.
answers.consequence_summary: Extreme aerodynamic torque snaps a solar panel mounting hinge during an atmospheric dip!
answers.learning_point: Exceeding aerodynamic pressure limits during aerobraking causes structural failure.

questions.story: Your direct chemical burn was successful, placing your heavy orbiter into an elliptical Mars orbit. However, your propellant tanks are 80% depleted.
questions.question: How will you prioritize the remaining station-keeping fuel?

answers.text: Remain in the high stable orbit to preserve reaction control fuel for 5 years.
answers.consequence_summary: Safe fuel reserves ensure a long mission lifetime and excellent broad weather monitoring.
answers.learning_point: High orbital altitudes experience virtually zero atmospheric drag, requiring minimal station-keeping fuel.

answers.text: Burn your remaining fuel to drop into a low 200 km mapping orbit.
answers.consequence_summary: Provides stunning high-resolution radar and camera images, but leaves zero fuel margin for emergency maneuvers.
answers.learning_point: Low orbits provide sharper imaging data but require active drag compensation.

questions.story: With aerobraking complete, your low circular orbit allows close observation. The science team wants to locate subsurface water ice.
questions.question: Which payload instrument will you activate as primary sensor?

source.title: NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Shallow Radar (SHARAD)

answers.consequence_summary: Bounces radio pulses through regolith, detecting buried ice sheets under Utopia Planitia!
answers.learning_point: Radar sounders reveal underground geology and ice reservoirs hidden beneath dust and rock.

answers.consequence_summary: Maps clay minerals and hydrated sulfates, charting where ancient rivers and lakes once pooled.
answers.learning_point: Spectrometers identify surface minerals by measuring the specific absorption wavelengths of reflected sunlight.

questions.story: From your high stable orbit, your spacecraft serves as an ideal telecommunications relay between Mars surface rovers and Earth.
questions.question: How will you configure the orbiter's relay transponders?

answers.text: Dedicate high-power UHF transceivers to relay rover data to Deep Space Network.
answers.consequence_summary: Your orbiter relays gigabytes of rover discoveries back to Earth, proving essential to the Mars program!
answers.learning_point: Orbiters serve as relay nodes because their high-gain dishes can transmit data to Earth much faster than a surface rover.

answers.text: Keep relays in low-power mode and prioritize the orbiter's own weather camera.
answers.consequence_summary: Generates steady regional weather maps, though surface teams miss key data transfer windows.
answers.learning_point: Balancing your own science with relay responsibilities is a common challenge for Mars orbiters.

questions.story: Low Mars orbit brings you within 200 km of the surface, but Martian atmospheric density fluctuates wildly during seasons.
questions.question: How will you protect the spacecraft from unexpected atmospheric density spikes?

source.title: NASA Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation

answers.text: Program autonomous safe-mode orbit boosts using momentum wheel desaturation.
answers.consequence_summary: Smart autonomous flight controls keep the spacecraft clear of thick air while capturing ultra-sharp radar maps!
answers.learning_point: Autonomous attitude control systems compensate for atmospheric fluctuations faster than commands sent across 20-minute signal delays.

answers.text: Rely solely on Earth ground controllers to send manual trajectory trims.
answers.consequence_summary: The 20-minute radio signal lag to Earth prevents timely correction, forcing an emergency altitude raise that ends early.
answers.learning_point: Radio signals take between 4 and 24 minutes to travel from Mars to Earth, making real-time manual piloting impossible.

questions.story: Your ground-penetrating radar has generated massive 3D data cubes of subsurface glaciers. Earth is currently 220 million kilometers away.
questions.question: Which communication subsystem will you utilize to transmit the radar maps?

source.title: NASA Deep Space Network Ka-Band Planetary Downlink

answers.text: 32 GHz Ka-band phased array pointed at Goldstone and Madrid DSN dishes.
answers.consequence_summary: High-frequency Ka-band beams down the entire 3D ice map in pristine detail, making headlines worldwide!
answers.learning_point: Ka-band frequencies offer four times higher data bandwidth than legacy X-band radio systems.

answers.text: Low-frequency X-band antenna with aggressive lossy image compression.
answers.consequence_summary: Conserves onboard electrical power, though some fine glacial boundary details are lost in compression.
answers.learning_point: Data compression reduces radio power demands at the cost of scientific resolution.

questions.story: A planet-encircling dust storm sweeps across the Southern hemisphere, blotting out surface features for the next two months.
questions.question: How will your mission team adapt to the global dust storm?

source.title: NASA Mars Global Dust Storm Observations

answers.text: Re-tune infrared sensors to track dust cloud altitudes and thermal heating.
answers.consequence_summary: Turns an environmental hazard into a landmark scientific study of how global dust storms alter Martian climate!
answers.learning_point: Infrared instruments can see through dust clouds that block visible light, revealing temperature structures.

answers.text: Put science payload into hibernation and wait for clear skies.
answers.consequence_summary: Protects spacecraft hardware safely, completing primary mapping after dust settles.
answers.learning_point: Safe-mode hibernation reduces thermal and electrical strain when environmental conditions degrade.

endings.title: Landmark Martian Discovery
endings.description: Exemplary mission execution! Your spacecraft successfully balanced aerobraking drag, solar power at Mars distance, and high-frequency Ka-band communications to map subsurface glacial water ice across Utopia Planitia.
endings.scientific_explanation: By pairing radar sounding with autonomous orbital attitude stabilization and Ka-band downlink, your spacecraft returned unprecedented geological datasets without exceeding budget.
endings.learning_point: Interplanetary missions succeed when orbital mechanics, thermal management, and autonomous systems operate in seamless concert.

endings.title: Reliable Long-Term Mars Workhorse
endings.description: Mission accomplished! Your conservative operational choices preserved battery life and fuel margins, allowing your spacecraft to serve as a vital communications relay and regional climate monitor for years.
endings.scientific_explanation: Choosing stable orbital altitudes and smart power hibernation protected critical spacecraft subsystems across harsh Martian seasons.
endings.learning_point: Reliable orbiters provide the foundational communications infrastructure enabling surface rover missions to succeed.

endings.title: Valuable Mars Geological Science
endings.description: Solid science return! Your spacecraft mapped ancient lakebed clay minerals and tracked atmospheric escape, providing essential clues about whether Mars once harbored life.
endings.scientific_explanation: Targeted spectrometer choices returned valuable mineral spectra despite bandwidth limitations during solar conjunction.
endings.learning_point: Spectroscopic measurements from orbit establish the chemical timeline of water and climate change on terrestrial planets.

endings.title: Partial Mission Return
endings.description: Mission completed with moderate scientific yield. Your orbiter remained healthy, but limited relay time and power constraints prevented returning full-resolution datasets.
endings.scientific_explanation: Conservative downlink schedules left high-volume raw radar and stereo image cubes stored in onboard memory.
endings.learning_point: Downlink bandwidth to Earth is a critical bottleneck for deep-space missions hundreds of millions of kilometers away.

endings.title: Orbital Emergency Safe Mode
endings.description: Emergency thruster burn executed! Due to radio delay from Earth, your orbiter dipped too deep into the atmosphere before safe software initiated an emergency orbit-raising burn.
endings.scientific_explanation: Light travel time to Mars prevented timely manual intervention, consuming remaining fuel reserves.
endings.learning_point: Deep-space robotic spacecraft require onboard autonomous fault detection to handle sudden dynamic hazards.

endings.title: Structural Failure in Aerobraking
endings.description: Telemetry lost during periapsis pass! Excessive aerodynamic drag torque damaged solar wing mountings, cutting off electrical power.
endings.scientific_explanation: Aerodynamic forces in thin upper atmospheres scale exponentially with velocity; unfeathered structures cannot withstand high supersonic dynamic pressures.
endings.learning_point: Never compromise structural orientation and safety margins during atmospheric entry and aerobraking maneuvers.
